QF.id: Clubbing, Set-Off and Carry Forward of Losses_23

question.text: Mr. Sanjay has the following incomes and losses in FY 2025-26: Non-speculative business income: Rs.4,00,000; Speculative business loss: Rs.1,50,000; Loss from card games (gambling): Rs.80,000; Income from horse racing: Rs.60,000. What is Sanjay's gross total income after permissible set-offs?

answer.text: Rs.2,30,000 — all losses set off against business income and horse racing income
Rs.4,60,000 — only speculative loss set off against business income
Rs.4,60,000 — speculative loss cannot be set off against non-speculative income; gambling loss cannot be set off against any income including horse racing; GTI = Rs.4,00,000 + Rs.60,000
Rs.3,80,000 — gambling loss set off against horse racing income; speculative loss carried forward

explanation.text: The Logic: Speculative business loss can only be set off against speculative business profits, and not against ordinary non-speculative business income, with any unabsorbed amount being carried forward for limited years for set-off against future speculative profits. Losses from activities such as lotteries, crossword puzzles, card games, gambling and similar wagering activities are not allowed to be set off against any other head of income, and they cannot be set off even against income from horse racing. Income from these activities is taxed under a special flat-rate regime without permitting deduction or loss set-off. Sanjay's non-speculative business income of Rs.4,00,000 and horse-racing income of Rs.60,000 therefore remain in his gross total income, yielding Rs.4,60,000. The Trap: Setting the speculative business loss against ordinary business income breaches the rule that speculative losses are ring-fenced. Allowing the gambling/card-game loss to be set off against horse-racing income misreads the absolute disallowance applicable to such losses. Setting the gambling loss against general business income is similarly not permitted. Note: The cited workbook chapter supports the speculative-loss ring-fencing rule, but does not explicitly state that card-game / gambling losses are disallowed against all other income (including horse-racing income), nor does it spell out the flat-rate Section 115BB regime referenced in this explanation. The framing above reflects the general Income-tax Act treatment of speculative losses and Section 115BB-type incomes rather than a direct workbook citation.
